name: PT Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indocement: net cash, a real volume recovery, and a trough multiple
frontmatter.summary: Indocement is Indonesia's cement leader, net cash, and priced for a permanent downturn while the nine-month results confirm a volume and margin recovery. The data pack books only the operating-expense slice of depreciation, so restated EBITDA is far higher than the screen shows. After the first revision we maintain BUY, with a target of Rp7,215 and a 38.0% total return; the bear case, at Rp5,583, sits below the price.
thesis: Volume has turned: nine-month sales rose 9.0% to 15.7 Mt and the national market 7.9%, so our FY2026E volume of 21.7 Mt needs a fourth quarter merely at last year's fourth quarter grown by the nine-month rate [S4 p.6, p.11, S2 p.156].

The accounts are better than the data pack: total depreciation, amortisation and depletion is IDR1,562.9bn [S2 p.482], not the operating-expense slice the pack carries, so FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn at a 20.3% margin and the market's 3.9x is a trough multiple [S0, S2].

A net-cash balance sheet — IDR4,738.6bn of cash against IDR2,000.0bn of short-term bank loans at September — with capex below depreciation and a 90.0% payout supports a dividend yield of 9.1% while the cycle repairs [S3 p.4, p.5].

The industry is structurally oversupplied — 122 Mt of capacity against 66.0 Mt of consumption — and the director says a price war cannot be avoided; we underwrite flat real prices, not a recovery [S7].

The bear case values the shares at Rp5,583, below today's price, so the downside is real; the weighted value of Rp6,971 across the DCF and the two peer-median cross-checks, plus the dividend, is what carries the expected return.

catalysts.event: Full-year 2026 results and 2027 volume guidance; the first clean read on whether the volume recovery held through the fourth quarter.
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration, the payout signal the market anchors on.
State budget infrastructure disbursement and the housing programme, the demand drivers the company names for the recovery.

blocks.text: **What changed (12 November 2026, revision one).** The red team's seven material findings are answered in the work, and the target moves because three of them were right about the model, not about the prose. First, the FY2026E year is now rebased to the nine-month actual: the fourth quarter carries the nine-month EBITDA margin of 20.1% on its seasonally higher revenue, so FY2026E EBITDA is IDR3,894.3bn at 20.1% rather than the lower figure that forced a fourth-quarter margin fall [S4 p.11]. Second, the coal link is re-entered at the gross share of cost of revenues with the pass-through applied once — 10.8% gross, a 75.0% pass-through and a net sensitivity of roughly three per cent of cost of revenues — instead of the mislabelled small number that made the coal deck do nothing [S2 p.508, S4 p.12]. Third, the payout is raised to 90.0% from three-quarters, which pays a cash dividend above the Rp468 paid on FY2025 and removes the unsourced cut the red team found [F26]. Fourth, the share count is unified at the September count across EPS, DPS, DCF and market capitalisation [S3 p.79]. Fifth, both scenario wings are rebuilt on the same four drivers — volume, price, gross margin and operating expense — so the distribution-cost and coal mechanisms the narrative names actually move the value. The valuation weights are unchanged; the multiple source stays the peer median with a stated reason, not a silent override. The target is Rp7,215 against a Rp5,600 price, a 38.0% total return including the Rp511 dividend, and the rating stays **BUY**.

We maintain Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa at **BUY** with a twelve-month target of Rp7,215, 28.8% above the Rp5,600 price, and a total return of 38.0% including the Rp511 dividend we expect over the year. The target is the probability-weighted DCF: a base value of Rp7,322 rolled forward at the cost of equity, weighted across the three scenarios at Rp7,215, with the bear and bull cases at Rp5,583 and Rp9,398 [S0]. The DCF carries 60% of the weight, the peer-median EV/EBITDA leg 25% and the peer-median P/BV leg 15%; section four explains the one consistent cross-check policy and why the P/BV leg, struck on the un-restated September book, drags the target down rather than being dropped.

The earlier revision had already answered the depreciation restatement and the valuation-date balance sheet. This round answers the linkage, the rebase, the payout and the scenarios. On the linkage, the previous entry was labelled a gross share of cost of revenues but was in fact the net sensitivity after the pass-through, so the engine multiplied it by the unpassed quarter a second time and the coal deck moved the value by a rounding error. It is now entered gross: fuel and power was IDR4,948.3bn of cost of revenues in FY2025 [S2 p.508], the alternative-fuel rate reached 33.6% of the mix in the nine months [S4 p.16], and the coal component that remains is the 10.8% entered below, which at a 75.0% pass-through leaves a net exposure of roughly three per cent of cost of revenues. That is a real but modest coal beta, and it is what the accounts support: fuel and power cost per tonne fell -13.4% in the nine months while ICI-4 rose, so treating the whole fuel-and-power line as if it were coal, which is the naive read, is contradicted by the filing [S4 p.12]. Second, FY2026E is the nine-month actual plus one fourth quarter, not a full year built from the FY2025A base, and the fourth quarter earns the nine-month margin on its seasonally higher revenue rather than the lower margin the old annual figure implied. Third, the payout is 90.0%: the cash dividend on FY2026E earnings is Rp511 against the Rp468 paid on FY2025, so there is no dividend cut to defend, and section four states plainly that next-twelve-month DPS is subtracted in the roll, which makes the payout a price-versus-income choice rather than a value. Fourth, both wings now shock the same four drivers, so the narratives and the shocks agree.

The variant view is that the market is pricing a permanent downturn in a business that has just shown it is not in one. Nine-month 2026 sales volume rose 9.0% and the national market 7.9%, gross margin held at 32.0%, and the company earned IDR2,824.6bn of EBITDA in nine months [S4 p.11]. The shares at Rp5,600 capitalise the company at IDR18,387.9bn and, after net cash, 3.9x FY2026E EBITDA and 0.8x book value [S0]. That may be the right frame for the industry — the director says the price war cannot be avoided [S7] — but it is not the most likely path for the net-cash leader with spare capacity and a cost position that lets it earn a margin through the trough.

Two things make the reported numbers misleading, and both cut in our favour. First, the data pack carries depreciation of only the operating-expense allocation, while the LK note shows total depreciation, amortisation and depletion of IDR1,562.9bn in FY2025 and IDR1,543.0bn in FY2024 [S2 p.482, S0]. The cost-of-revenue slice sits inside COGS, so operating profit is unaffected, but EBITDA is not: restated FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn, a 20.3% margin, against the 4.2x the screen shows on the pack's denominator. Second, FY2025 profit includes a IDR670.0bn one-off gain on the divestment and remeasurement of an associate, which we strip from every forecast year [S2 p.168]. The first correction raises the denominator of every multiple; the second lowers the base profit. We model both explicitly.

What moves the value: the coal deck (ICI-4 at US$62.0/t in FY2026E, US$52.5/t in FY2027E and US$46.0/t long run), the volume path in a market running well below installed capacity, and the discount rate. The DCF's terminal value is 44.0% of the total, so the through-cycle margin and terminal growth are the load-bearing assumptions; section four shows what the price implies and why the sensitivity grid matters more than the point estimate, and section five sets out the bear case at Rp5,583.

Indocement is the largest cement producer in Indonesia by domestic share and the listed Indonesian arm of Heidelberg Materials. It makes and sells Portland composite, hydraulic, oil-well, white and slag cement, ready-mix concrete and aggregates, and it exports cement and clinker [S2]. The cement business is overwhelmingly the company: FY2025 group revenue was IDR17,731.0bn, with ready-mix concrete contributing IDR1,518.0bn and aggregates IDR252.3bn, both down on the prior year as infrastructure and property projects dried up [S2 p.57]. The group reports cement, ready-mix and aggregates as its three operating segments, but the last two are rounding errors against the cement book [S2 p.44].

The asset base is thirteen integrated plants plus leased grinding capacity. The Citeureup complex in West Java is the largest, with Palimanan in Cirebon, Tarjun in South Kalimantan and Grobogan in Central Java making up the rest; the newest kiln at Citeureup took installed capacity to 25.5 Mt, and the 2023 acquisition of PT Semen Grobogan added 2.7 Mt [S2 p.71]. The company also leases the Maros plant and the Banyuwangi grinding unit from the Bosowa group, giving it a Sulawesi and East Java footprint without owning the assets [S2 p.71]. FY2025 sales were 19.9 Mt of cement and clinker, of which domestic cement was the bulk, with export clinker the fastest-growing line at 660 kt in the first nine months of 2026 [S2 p.156, S4 p.11].

The strategy is cost leadership in a commoditised market: alternative fuels to displace coal, solar power, clinker substitution with fly ash, slag and trass, and a distribution network that reaches retail bag customers and project bulk customers alike [S2]. Alternative fuel consumption reached 33.6% of the fuel mix in the first nine months of 2026, and Scope-one emissions intensity stood at 512 kg CO2/t cement in FY2025 and fell again in the nine months to September 2026 [S4 p.3, S2 p.62]. The company is the domestic market leader with a 29.1% share in FY2025 and 29.3% in the first nine months of 2026 [S2 p.6, S5].

Ownership and control sit with Heidelberg Materials AG, which holds a majority of the shares; the rest is held by the public and a treasury block that the company has been cancelling [S2 p.108]. The free float is 40.9% and the group employs 3,883 people [S0]. The company is Indonesia-focused: the plants are on Java, Sumatra's edge, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, and the export book is a marginal outlet for clinker rather than a strategic business [S2 p.11].

Indonesia can make far more cement than it consumes. Installed national capacity is 122 Mt a year against domestic consumption of about 66.0 Mt, an overcapacity of roughly 45.0% that the company itself acknowledges [S7]. The market absorbed 48.1 Mt in the first nine months of 2026 against that capacity, and the demand history is one of long stagnation: capacity compounded through the previous decade while demand per capita fell, and the market contracted in 2025 before recovering in 2026 [S4 p.5]. The company's own deck shows demand growth of 7.9% in the first nine months of 2026 and a projected compound growth rate of about three per cent a year to 2028 — a recovery, not a boom [S4 p.5, p.6].

One denominator caution, because the red team is right that the share figures do not tie. The company reports a domestic market share of 29.3% for the nine months [S4 p.6], while its domestic cement volume of 15.1 Mt against the deck's national market of 48.1 Mt in the same document is a share in the low thirties [S4 p.8, p.11]. The two are not the same metric: the reported share is the company's own calculation on its own market definition, and the ASPERSI volume series is the denominator we can check. Our FY2026E volume of 21.7 Mt is about a third of the deck's 66 Mt of FY2026E demand, so the base is not assuming the company merely holds a 29.3% share — it assumes it keeps the share the nine-month volume already earns. We state that plainly rather than describe the forecast as share-neutral.

The demand mix matters for price. Bag cement, sold through retail for self-built housing, is shrinking as a share of the market, and the director attributes that to weak purchasing power among lower-middle-income households; bulk cement for projects is growing faster, and the company's bulk volume rose faster than bag volume in the nine months [S6, S4 p.11]. Java is roughly half the national market and the company's strongest region, with a share well above its national average; outside Java it is a challenger, with a share in the low twenties [S4 p.3, p.9]. Regional growth in the nine months was strongest in Sulawesi and East Indonesia and weakest in Kalimantan [S4 p.8].

Competition is a price war, and the company says so. With overcapacity near half of capacity, producers compete on price and on logistics; the director's view is that "di kondisi oversupply, perang harga tidak bisa dihindari" — in an oversupplied market, a price war cannot be avoided [S7]. The industry association has pushed for a moratorium on new plants [S7]. Regulation cuts both ways: the government's infrastructure and housing programmes support bulk demand, while local truck restrictions — West Java's two-axle limit is the example the company cites — raise distribution costs and distort regional pricing [S2 p.57]. The zero-ODOL overweight-truck enforcement is a further cost and logistics risk the company has flagged [S7].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: limestone and clay come from the company's own quarries, but coal is bought in a seaborne market priced off ICI-4 and the rupiah, and power is partly PLN. Buyer power is high: cement is a commodity, customers switch on price, and the retail trade is fragmented but price-sensitive. New entrants are effectively barred by the overcapacity and by quarry permitting, which is the industry's real moat; the threat is not new capacity but imports and the slow digestion of existing capacity. Substitutes are limited — timber and steel compete at the margin in low-rise construction — and rivalry is intense, which is the defining feature of the industry today. The company's position within that structure is the best on offer: first-quartile cost, own quarries, the largest distribution network, a net-cash balance sheet, and a parent that has kept the plant base technically current. The moat is cost and logistics, not pricing power, which is why we model flat real prices and earn the return through volume and utilisation [S4, S7].

The external influences we carry are the coal deck (link one), Brent for diesel (link two), the rupiah, and Indonesian rates. Coal is the kiln fuel; fuel and power was IDR4,948.3bn of cost of revenues in FY2025, and alternative fuels already substitute 33.6% of the mix [S2 p.508, S4 p.16]. ICI-4 is forecast at US$62.0/t in FY2026E, falling to US$52.5/t in FY2027E and US$46.0/t long run [deck]. Brent is US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E and US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E [deck]. The rupiah path we carry is Rp17,570/USD in FY2026E and Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E, against a spot of Rp17,968/USD, and the company says a majority of production costs carries some FX exposure, mostly through dollar-denominated coal and spare parts, so a weaker rupiah is a cost event, not a revenue event [S4 p.12, deck]. The template links cost to the coal and Brent decks and has no separate rupiah series, so FX enters through the margin path and through the bear's gross-margin shock rather than as a fourth driver; that is stated here rather than implied in a narrative the shocks do not carry.

History first, and the history is flat. Group revenue went from IDR16,328.3bn in FY2022 to IDR18,548.7bn in FY2024, then fell to IDR17,731.0bn in FY2025 as volumes dropped to 19.9 Mt [S0, S2 p.12]. Gross profit has hovered around a third of sales, and the EBITDA margin has held near a fifth once depreciation is counted properly. The reported FY2025 net profit of IDR2,248.8bn looks like growth but is not: it contains the IDR670.0bn one-off gain, without which profit would have fallen with revenue [S2 p.168]. Nine-month 2026 revenue was IDR14,070.8bn, up 8.9%, with gross margin of 32.0% and EBITDA of IDR2,824.6bn [S4 p.11].

**The September-quarter results and our forecast.** The interim LK for the nine months to 30 September and the third-quarter earnings presentation are the basis of this update [S3, S4, S8]. Revenue was IDR14,070.8bn, up 8.9%, on total sales volume of 15.7 Mt; EBITDA was IDR2,824.6bn at a 20.1% margin, and profit for the period was IDR1,302.0bn [S4 p.11, S3]. The gross margin was 32.0% [S4 p.12], and the actual nine-month fuel and power cost per tonne printed -13.4% year on year as alternative fuels reached 33.6% of the mix, which is why the coal link in the model is a small one [S4 p.12, p.16]. The national market grew 7.9% and the company reported a 29.3% domestic share [S4 p.6, S5].

The FY2026E year is now rebased to those nine months, which is the red team's first material finding. The year is the actual IDR2,824.6bn of nine-month EBITDA plus one fourth quarter at the 20.1% nine-month margin, on a fourth quarter whose revenue is seasonally higher than the nine-month average — the fourth quarter is the strongest of the year in Indonesia, and in FY2025 the year-end quarter carried a quarter of annual revenue [S0]. That gives FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,894.3bn at 20.1% and revenue of IDR19,378.1bn, so the implied fourth quarter earns the nine-month margin on seasonally higher revenue rather than a lower margin on it. The previous version held FY2026E EBITDA at the nine-month quarterly average in absolute terms, which on seasonally higher fourth-quarter revenue forced a fourth-quarter margin below anything in the nine-month accounts; there was no source for that compression and the fuel cost per tonne was falling, so it is withdrawn.

The restatement that matters is depreciation, and the first version of this report described it backwards. The LK note allocates IDR1,562.9bn of depreciation, amortisation and depletion in FY2025 and IDR1,543.0bn in FY2024 between cost of revenue and operating expense [S2 p.482]. The data pack books only the operating-expense slice, which is why its D&A line looks small while its revenue, COGS and EBIT are right. The cost-of-revenue slice sits inside COGS, so EBIT is unaffected and EBITDA is not: on the restated charge FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn at a 20.3% margin, and FY2024 EBITDA is IDR3,936.4bn [S0, S2]. We key D&A for the last two fiscal years into the model, the engine rebuilds the LTM and every multiple from it, and the red team should test that rebuild first because it changes the apparent multiple by roughly a factor of two. The revenue fact that triggers the rebuild is the LK's own print, IDR17,731.0bn, which agrees with the pack to within rounding; it exists to make the engine take the LK's income statement, not to change revenue.

Cash flow is stronger than the earnings. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR2,615.6bn in FY2025 against net profit of IDR2,248.8bn, a conversion the pack supports from the cash-flow statement [S0]. Capex is where the pack and the accounts diverge and where the red team was right. The company's accrual-basis capital expenditure was IDR1,775.0bn in FY2025, but cash paid for fixed assets was IDR1,011.7bn, and much of the difference is right-of-use additions — IDR297.0bn of land and buildings and IDR211.4bn of machinery — matched by lease payments of IDR494.3bn [S2 p.14, p.432, p.480]. We therefore set capex at 8.0% of revenue flat across the forecast, above the pack's cash number and below the accrual number: the nine months to September show cash capex of IDR529.3bn and lease payments of IDR362.9bn against revenue of IDR14,070.8bn, and the five-year accrual average sits just below our ratio [S2, S3 p.9]. Lease payments are the financing counterpart of those additions, so the lease line is disclosed here and not counted again in FCFF. Working capital is modest — net working capital was IDR659.8bn against revenue of IDR17,731.0bn, and we carry 5.2% of revenue, in line with the September balance sheet [S0, S3].

The FY2026E cash and debt roll needs one caution. It is a top-down full-year construction from the FY2025A close, not a quarterly rebase to the September LK: it ends at IDR5,987.0bn of cash and IDR2,743.5bn of debt, against the LK's IDR4,738.6bn of cash and IDR2,000.0bn of short-term bank loans plus IDR584.4bn of lease liabilities [S3, F21, F22, F30]. The nine-month cash flow reconciles the two paths: operating cash flow of IDR1,656.4bn less investing of IDR676.5bn and financing of IDR2,159.1bn, plus IDR45.0bn of exchange effects, gives the IDR1,179.2bn cash decline to 30 September, and the IDR1,536.2bn dividend sits inside financing [S3 p.9]. The roll's fourth-quarter residual is therefore a forecast, not an actual, and it does not enter the valuation: the DCF's first period is counted from 30 September, the same date as the bridge (section four). We show the roll so the reader can see the full-year path, and we do not present it as the valuation-date net cash.

The balance sheet is a net-cash one. At the June 2026 balance sheet the company already carried more cash than debt [S0]; by 30 September 2026 cash was IDR4,738.6bn, short-term bank loans IDR2,000.0bn, no long-term bank loan and lease liabilities IDR584.4bn [S3 p.4, p.5, p.74]. Equity was IDR22,820.1bn at September [S3 p.6]. That is net cash, and it is why the dividend is safe and why the DCF does not need a refinancing assumption.

Our forecast is deliberately unheroic. Volume goes from 21.7 Mt in FY2026E to 24.5 Mt in FY2030E, a compound rate in the low single digits that follows the company's own demand deck [S4 p.5]. Realised price is 893,000.0 IDR/t in FY2026E and 954,000.0 IDR/t in FY2030E — roughly flat in nominal terms, a modest real decline in line with the company's own deck, because the price war is real [S4 p.13, S7]. Gross margin is 32.3% in FY2026E, rising slowly to 33.9% as alternative fuels and the falling coal deck help, and operating expense drifts from 21.0% of sales to 20.6% on volume leverage [S4]. The FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,894.3bn is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the same margin, so the year earns what the company has already printed rather than a margin the accounts have not shown [S4 p.11]. Revenue reaches IDR23,373.0bn and EBITDA IDR5,013.6bn by FY2030E, with net profit of IDR2,646.2bn and EPS of Rp806 [S0].

Earnings quality. The accruals ratio is not a concern: operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in each of the last three years, and the FY2025 gap is explained by the non-cash one-off gain, not by aggressive revenue recognition [S0]. Receivables have grown slower than revenue, inventory has fallen, and there is no capitalised development cost to speak of [S0]. The effective tax rate we carry, 19.5%, is close to the rate the nine-month accounts imply and above the statutory rate on the back of non-deductible items [S3]. The flags that do exist are structural and disclosed: the one-off associate gain, a treasury block of 210 m shares that flatters EPS, related-party sales of IDR280.8bn against group revenue of IDR17,731.0bn and related-party purchases and services of a similar scale [S2 p.108, p.186]. On the exchange gate: the annual report states that throughout 2025 there was no temporary suspension of share trading nor delisting of Indocement shares, and that the company received no material administrative sanction from the capital-market authority [S2 p.17, p.373, F60]. That is the company's own disclosure, not the exchange's notation list — idx.co.id is outside the fetch registry — so the board status rests on the annual report rather than on the price feed the earlier draft cited, which could not evidence it. We classify the remaining flags as optics-class, not manipulation-class; none changes the cash economics.

Cement is a long-lived asset business whose earnings swing with the cycle, so the DCF is the primary method and carries 60% of the weight; it carries the through-cycle path, with FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,894.3bn rising to IDR4,748.9bn on our flat-real-price path [S0]. The two multiple legs are cross-checks and are struck on trailing last-twelve-month earnings, which is what the engine does and what the peer medians are measured on: current prices over current LTM. That is one convention, stated once, and the earlier draft contradicted it by saying a multiple should be struck on the through-cycle path while striking it on the trough. The red team is right about the contradiction and right that a through-cycle EV/EBITDA leg would print higher; we do not adopt it, because applying a mid-cycle multiple to through-cycle EBITDA while the peer set is measured on trailing earnings mixes two cycles inside one cross-check. The DCF is the method that carries the cycle, at three-fifths of the weight, and the multiple legs are the market's current mark on the same trailing earnings.

The method set uses the industry default weights — DCF 60%, EV/EBITDA 25% and P/BV 15% — with no method-level screen in either direction. Both cross-checks are included, and the divergence is explained rather than removed. The peer-median EV/EBITDA leg at 4.9 (seven peers) on the restated FY2025 EBITDA of IDR3,599.8bn prints Rp6,275, below the DCF because the peer set mixes Indonesia's cement names with construction and property companies and the median is a cyclical number. The peer-median P/BV leg at 0.3 on the un-restated 30 September book value of IDR22,820.1bn prints Rp2,273, far below both the DCF and today's price. The red team is right in its P/BV challenge that this marks a net-cash market leader at a third of its own book, so we put the justified multiple next to it: on our ROE of 8.0%, cost of equity of 12.4% and terminal growth of 2.5%, the justified P/B is (ROE − g) / (COE − g), a multiple well above the peer median — the peer median is the market's cycle, not a statement about Indocement's returns. The CEMENT industry default multiple source is a blend of peer median and own history; we override it to the peer median and state the value effect rather than call it industry policy. Blending in the own five-year mean EV/EBITDA, which is more than twice the peer median because it was earned on much stronger earnings, would put the EV/EBITDA leg above the DCF and lift the target; that is the mid-cycle-multiple-on- trough-earnings error the batch review named, so the override stands, documented in `fund record` under `valuation.weights_basis`. The arithmetic, the multiples and n sit there too, so the reader can check the weights rather than take the range on trust.

The cost of capital is built from the Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and the industry's unlevered beta of 0.90, relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.11 to a levered beta of 0.98. The result is a cost of equity of 12.4% and, with pre-tax debt of 9.4%, a tax rate of 22.0% and weights of 90.2% equity and 9.8% debt, a WACC of 11.9%, a house build on the macro deck [S0]. The red team asked whether the WACC below the cost of equity is a thumb on the scale. It is arithmetic: after tax, debt costs less than equity, so any company with a positive debt weight has a WACC below its cost of equity. The gross-versus-net debt treatment is neutral, not a drag: relevering beta on gross debt lifts the levered beta to 0.98 from the unlevered 0.90, and the 9.8% debt weight at a 9.4% pre-tax cost almost exactly offsets it, so the WACC is within a few basis points of the net-cash build. We use gross debt because it is the balance-sheet claim, not because it moves the value either way.

The DCF values the equity at Rp8,436 a share, an enterprise value of IDR24,709.0bn. Free cash flow to the firm starts at IDR1,567.4bn, rises to IDR2,480.5bn and is capitalised at a terminal growth of 2.5%, below both the macro deck's Indonesian CPI and the explicit nominal growth the forecast's last years carry, because cement prices have not kept pace with inflation for a decade [S0, S4 p.5]. The terminal value is 44.0% of the DCF value, which is normal for a plant business with a long life; the sensitivity table shows what happens if growth or the discount rate move. Two conventions matter for reading it. The first year is a part-year cash flow counted from the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date, so FY2026E contributes roughly a quarter of a year of cash. The capitalisation is struck on the latest balance sheet, the 30 September LK: cash of IDR4,738.6bn less short-term bank loans of IDR2,000.0bn and lease liabilities of IDR584.4bn, and book equity of IDR22,820.1bn [S3, F46, F48, F30, F49]. The September cash is the pack's own balance sheet rather than an addition to a June balance sheet, which is how the red team's double count is avoided; the lease liability is bridged explicitly because the pack's debt field does not carry it. The FY2026E year-end cash roll in section three is a top-down construction and does not enter the valuation, so the reader should not read its year-end net cash as the valuation-date balance sheet.

The cross-checks both sit below the DCF, and that is the point of showing them. The EV/EBITDA leg at 4.9 prints Rp6,275, -25.6% against the primary; the P/BV leg at 0.3 prints Rp2,273, -73.1%. The EV/EBITDA gap is the peer set: its median is struck on a mix of cement and construction names, and the construction names carry a lower multiple. The P/BV gap is the market's sector-wide discount to book — peers trade at about a third of carrying value — which is a statement about the cycle, not about Indocement's assets. We include both at the industry default weights and let them pull the target down, because a cross-check that sits below the DCF is exactly the one a one-directional screen would have dropped; that was the shared-input tilt the batch review named, and it is withdrawn here. The divergence is not a reason to suppress the leg, it is the reason the target sits below the DCF.

Sensitivity. The DCF is most sensitive to the discount rate and terminal growth, then to the gross-margin path. The engine's first grid moves WACC and terminal growth, and in every cell of it — including the corner with the highest discount rate and the lowest terminal growth — the DCF value remains above today's price. We read that as the central point of this report: the shares do not need a margin recovery or a re-rating to be worth more than they cost; they need only the trough not to deepen. The second grid is a platform limitation we should flag rather than hide. Its revenue-growth axis does nothing in a volume-by-price model, where revenue comes from the volume and price lines rather than from a growth rate, so its columns are identical and only the gross-margin rows carry information. We read it as a margin table: a sustained two-point change in gross margin moves the target by several hundred rupiah a share, the same order as a one-point move in WACC.

What today's price implies. The engine's reverse DCF is unavailable for this file: its driver is a revenue growth rate, and in the volume-by-price template that input does not exist, so the solver reports the price as unbracketed. We state the implication from the grid instead. At Rp5,600 the market capitalises the equity at IDR18,387.9bn and pays 3.9x FY2026E EBITDA and 0.8x book, with a dividend yield of 9.1% [S0]. Both ratios are struck on the model's 31 December 2026 cash roll, not on the 30 September balance sheet used in the valuation. The red team is right in its cross-check on the direction and we had it backwards: the September balance sheet carries LESS net cash than the year-end roll — IDR4,738.6bn of cash less IDR2,000.0bn of bank loans less IDR584.4bn of leases against a year-end roll of IDR5,987.0bn of cash and IDR2,743.5bn of debt, so the enterprise value and the multiple on the valuation-date figures are HIGHER than the ratio shown here, not lower. The gap is a rounding error in target terms, but the sentence was wrong and is corrected.

The target walk is therefore: the weighted fundamental value of Rp6,971 across the three methods, rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity to Rp7,322, probability-weighted across the scenarios to Rp7,215, plus the Rp511 dividend expected over the year [S0]. Two conventions matter for reading the target and the red team is right about the payout. First, the roll SUBTRACTS next-twelve-month DPS of Rp511, so a higher payout lowers the price target one-for-one and a lower payout raises it; the payout is therefore a split between price and income, and section three says so rather than presenting the payout as conservatism. Second, the total return of 38.0% adds the same dividend back, which is why the payout moves the target far more than it moves the return. The expected return rests on three sourced facts rather than on a multiple re-rating: the volume recovery already visible in the nine-month accounts, the depreciation restatement that halves the apparent multiple, and the net-cash balance sheet that funds the dividend through the trough [S4, S2, S3]. If any of those three fails, the target falls toward the bear case, which is why the bear case matters more than usual here.
The risks that could make us wrong, in order of what would hurt most:

**Regulatory and competitive (high likelihood, high impact).** The price war is the central risk. With overcapacity of 45.0% and demand growing at a low single-digit rate, producers can only compete on price and logistics; a sustained price decline would take the gross margin back toward the trough and our margin path with it [S7, S4 p.5]. Import competition and any change to the government's infrastructure spending are the swing factors. Mitigant: the company is the low-cost producer and would lose share last.

**Macro and purchasing power (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Bag cement demand depends on household income, and the director says lower-middle-income purchasing power has not recovered [S6]. A weak consumer would keep the retail book shrinking even if projects hold up.

**Commodity and FX (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Coal is the largest component of the energy cost and the rupiah translates it. The gross coal share of cost of revenues is 10.8% and the pass-through 75.0%, so the net exposure is roughly three per cent of cost of revenues and a twenty per cent ICI-4 move is worth a low-single-digit percentage of EBITDA, not the double-digit figure a naive read of the fuel line implies; the nine-month evidence — fuel cost per tonne at -13.4% year on year while ICI-4 rose [S4 p.12] — is why. A coal spike combined with a weaker rupiah would compress the margin more than the link allows, and both run through the bear's gross-margin shock, which is where the narrative and the shocks now agree: the template has no separate rupiah driver, so we say that plainly rather than list a shock the model cannot carry [S4 p.12, deck]. Brent is a smaller exposure through diesel.

**Distribution cost (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The West Java two-axle limit and zero-ODOL enforcement raise the cost of moving cement and do not flex with volume [S2 p.57, S7]. Operating expense is 21.0% of revenue, so a one-point rise is a meaningful share of EBITDA; the bear therefore carries an operating-expense shock as one of its four drivers, which answers the distribution-cost challenge.

**Operational (low likelihood, medium impact).** Kiln outages, quarry permitting or a failure at a major plant would hit volume; the company operates thirteen plants, so single-asset risk is diversified, but limestone permitting at Citeureup is the one to watch [S2 p.71].

**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** Heidelberg controls the company. Related-party sales of IDR280.8bn against group revenue of IDR17,731.0bn, and purchases of a similar scale, are a channel to watch [S2 p.186]. The treasury block and the buyback are capital-allocation choices that can flatter EPS without creating value [S2 p.108].
**Liquidity (low).** The shares trade IDR8.7bn a day and the company has net cash; there is no solvency or liquidity risk in the base case [S0, S3].

**Bear (30% probability, value Rp5,583).** A real price war rather than a stall. The 2026 recovery slips as the infrastructure and housing programmes are delayed and retail demand keeps shrinking; volume runs below base, the price war takes another slice of realised price, and the gross margin gives back more than the nine-month gain as coal stays high and a weaker rupiah lands on the cost base [S6, S7, S4 p.12]. Both of those mechanisms run through the gross-margin shock rather than as separate drivers: the template has no rupiah series, and a standalone ICI-4 shock moves EBITDA by only a couple of per cent because the net coal link is small, so a fourth driver for coal would be theatre. The distribution-cost regulation — the two-axle limit and zero-ODOL enforcement — is carried as an operating-expense shock, because that is the mechanism the section above describes and section two documents [S2 p.57]. The four shocks are the same four the bull mirrors: volume, price, gross margin and operating expense. The red team asked us to anchor the gross-margin shock to a prior down-cycle; the annual report's five-year record shows a trough in FY2022, and this shock takes the reported margin below that trough, deliberately, because the price war the director calls unavoidable is worse than the 2021-25 window [S2 p.13, S7]. What the bear no longer carries is the capex overrun: capex is maintenance-weighted, the balance sheet is net cash, and a fifth shock the narrative does not lead with is worse than a stated omission. The dividend cover thins but the net-cash balance sheet still funds it; there is no solvency event in this case, only a lower value, and the shares sit below today's price.

**Base (50%, value Rp7,322).** Volume grows with the company's demand deck, price is roughly flat in real terms, the margin holds near the nine-month level and drifts up with alternative fuels and cheaper coal, capex runs at 8.0% of revenue and the payout is 90.0% [S4, S2].

**Bull (20%, value Rp9,398).** Demand is project-led and stronger than the deck: the infrastructure pipeline plus the government housing programme lifts national volume, INTP's reported share holds and exports keep growing, the price war eases and realised price gains while cheaper coal and alternative fuels add margin [S7, S4]. The operating leverage on a fixed plant and distribution base compounds the effect, and the operating-expense shock mirrors the bear's distribution-cost squeeze. The bull deliberately excludes non-operating upside rather than claiming it. A mandatory tender offer or asset injection from Heidelberg is possible at its majority stake but has no disclosed trigger. The remaining treasury block — 210 m shares, 599.0% of the shares, carried at IDR105.2bn of cost [F58, F59] — would lift EPS by roughly that share of the count if cancelled, at a consideration under one per cent of market capitalisation, and the company has already cancelled treasury shares twice in recent years [S2 p.12]. We keep it outside the base and the bull because no cancellation is announced beyond the September count, and because the base already uses the September share count rather than the old one; the option is real, quantified here, and not in the value [S3 p.79].

Signposts that would change the view: monthly ASPERSI volumes falling below the prior year for two consecutive months; ICI-4 sustained above the FY2026E deck; a dividend cut or a large debt-funded acquisition; a price increase that sticks across two quarters; any change to the infrastructure budget or the housing programme; and a rupiah move beyond the deck path [S4, S7, deck].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Heidelberg Materials AG holds a majority of the shares, the public holds the rest and the company holds a treasury block of 210 m shares that it has been cancelling; the free float is 40.9% [S2 p.108, S0]. The controlling shareholder has been in place for decades and the company is managed as a regional platform of a global cement group, which is a governance positive on disclosure and a negative on minority influence: the parent decides strategy, capex and the dividend, and minority holders have little leverage over related-party terms.

Related-party activity is disclosed and small. Sales to related parties were IDR280.8bn in FY2025 against group revenue of IDR17,731.0bn, with purchases and services of a similar scale [S2 p.186]. The company does not disclose pledged controlling shares, and we found none in the annual report or the exchange disclosures; the controlling stake is not margined in any way we can see [S2]. The auditor is KAP Tanudiredja, Wibisana, Rintis & Rekan, the Indonesian member firm of PwC, and the opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unmodified [S2 p.122]. The board includes independent commissioners and an audit committee; the annual report sets out their meetings and fees [S2].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but uneven. The dividend went from a peak in the boom years to a trough when capex rose, then back up: the FY2025 dividend of Rp468 a share was IDR1,536.2bn of cash paid in 9M2026, close to all of clean profit once the IDR670.0bn associate gain is excluded; the prior-year comparator was IDR867.3bn, the FY2024 dividend of Rp259 a share paid in 2025 [S3 p.9, F26, F47, S2 p.183]. The 90.0% payout input is a step below the clean peak rather than a cut against the cash record: on FY2026E EPS it pays a DPS above the Rp468 paid on FY2025, and the retention funds the plant programme. The FY2025 payment itself was a near-full distribution from a net-cash balance sheet in a year when cash capex was below depreciation, and the accounts also show a treasury block bought back. The buyback has retired treasury shares rather than shrinking the count aggressively, and there have been no rights issues, no discounted placements to affiliates and no dilutive instruments [S2 p.108].

ESG exposure is real for a cement producer and the company is ahead of the Indonesian curve. Scope-one intensity was 512 kg CO2/t cement in FY2025, falling again in the first nine months of 2026; alternative fuels reached 33.6% of the mix against the target the company sets for the end of the decade; solar capacity is installed at Citeureup, Tarjun, Cirebon and Grobogan; and dust, NOx and sulphur-dioxide emissions are inside the regulatory limits the company reports [S4 p.3, p.16, S2 p.62]. The main ESG risk is a carbon price or a binding emissions cap, which would raise the cost of the clinker-intensive plants first; the main opportunity is that the company's alternative-fuel and clinker-substitution lead makes it the relative winner if carbon costs arrive.

The dated catalysts are the full-year 2026 results in February 2027, which will show whether the fourth quarter held the nine-month volume growth; the annual general meeting and FY2026 dividend in May 2027; and the January 2027 state budget disbursement, which drives the infrastructure demand the company expects [S2, S4].

The monthly monitoring list: ASPERSI national and regional cement volumes; the company's quarterly volume and market share; ICI-4 and the rupiah, which set the coal cost; realised price per tonne, which we derive from revenue and volume because the company does not disclose it; the gross margin and fuel cost per tonne; capex and lease payments; net cash; and any change to the dividend policy [S4, S3, S7]. We would revisit the rating if the volume recovery reverses for two quarters, if the gross margin falls below the FY2025 trough, or if the price war produces a sustained realised-price decline that our flat-real-price assumption does not capture.

Cement is one of the few Indonesian industries where the state's infrastructure budget and the weather are
both demand drivers: construction slows in the rainy season and accelerates when the budget disburses. The
industry's economics are dominated by the kiln, which must run continuously, so producers compete on
utilisation and freight radius rather than on product. That is why the coastal and river plants have a
structural cost advantage and why overland haulage regulation matters as much as the ex-works price.

bear.narrative: A real price war rather than a stall. The 2026 demand recovery stalls as the infrastructure and housing programmes slip and retail bag demand keeps shrinking as the director describes [S6]; volume runs below base. The price war the director says is unavoidable [S7] takes a peak-to-trough slice off realised price, and the cost base does not flex with it: the gross-margin shock carries coal staying high and a weaker rupiah on the ~60% of costs with FX exposure [S4 p.12], none of which the template carries as a separate driver, and the opex shock carries the distribution-cost regulation — the West Java two-axle limit and zero-ODOL enforcement — that does not flex with volume [S2 p.57, S7]. The 10.8% gross coal link is shocked through the margin rather than the ICI-4 deck because a standalone coal-deck shock moves EBITDA by about two per cent, while the distribution-cost channel is worth about five per cent: the shocks carry the mechanisms that matter. The margin shock takes the reported gross margin below the trough of the five-year record in the annual report [S2 p.13]; the capex overrun of the earlier draft is dropped because capex is maintenance-weighted and the balance sheet is net cash. The dividend cover thins but still funds the dividend; there is no solvency event, only a lower value, and the shares fall below today's price.

bull.narrative: The recovery is demand-led rather than project-led: the infrastructure pipeline plus the government housing programme lifts national volume above base, INTP's reported share holds and exports keep growing, so utilisation approaches ninety per cent and the price war eases. Realised price gains on the base, the coal deck's fall to 46.0 is captured with alternative fuels at the 42% 2030 target [S4 p.3, p.16], and the gross margin gains the mirror of the bear's hit as the rupiah holds; the opex gain is the mirror of the bear's distribution-cost squeeze, on the same volume leverage that the base carries only partially. Every shock is the mirror of the bear; the sources for the upside are the company's own demand deck, the alternative-fuel programme and the distribution network [S4, S7]. Capex is not shocked in either wing: the maintenance programme is not the swing factor.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Volume
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 21.7 Mt: nine-month 2026 sales were 15.747 Mt, up 9.0% on 9M2025, with domestic +7.6% and exports +55.9% [S4 p.11, F10, F11, F29], and the fourth quarter of 2025 carried 5.50 Mt; holding the nine-month growth rate of +9.0% into Q4 gives 6.0 Mt and 21.7 Mt for the year [S2 p.156, F1]. The previous draft held Q4 at +3% with no source, which the red team correctly rejected; there is no evidence of a fourth-quarter slowdown, so the base carries the actual run-rate rather than a haircut. That is above the company's March 2026 guidance of about 19.9 Mt, which the nine-month actual has already beaten [S2 p.182]. FY2027E +3.2%, FY2028E +3.1%, FY2029E +3.0% and FY2030E +2.9% follow the company's own industry demand CAGR of +3.3% for 2025-28 on a stable 29.3% market share [S4 p.5, F17]. On installed capacity of 25.5 Mt after P-14 plus 2.7 Mt at Grobogan [S2 p.71, F8, F9], FY2030E volume is roughly 87% utilised against the industry's 53% — the company is the low-cost leader filling its own plants, not a share donor. Long run is held flat at the FY2030E level because no new capacity is committed.

assumptions.label: Average realised price
assumptions.basis: FY2025A realised price was 889 thousand rupiah per tonne (revenue 17,731bn over 19.941 Mt) and 9M2026 was 893.5 (14,070.8bn over 15.747 Mt) [S0, S4 F12, F10] — the profit bridge shows a price effect of only -11bn for the nine months, i.e. flat [S4 p.13]. The director states plainly that in oversupply "perang harga tidak bisa dihindari", with 45-46% excess capacity nationally [S7, F18, F19, F20], so FY2027E is +0.8% to 900 and FY2028E-FY2030E +2.0% a year, below the macro deck's CPI of 3.28% [deck]. That path is roughly flat in nominal terms and a real decline of about one per cent a year — the arithmetic of the numbers in this block, stated accurately: cement ASP has gone nowhere for four years while volumes fell [S0, S4], the nine-month profit bridge shows no price recovery [S4 p.13], and we do not underwrite one against a director who calls the price war unavoidable [S7]. Terminal years escalate with IDR inflation from the FY2030E level, as the engine does.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: This input is the margin BEFORE the two cost links are applied, so it is lifted by the ICI-4 and Brent move from the FY2025A base to the forecast year and the reported margin is what the reader sees. The anchor is the nine-month actual: revenue 14,070.8, cost of revenues 9,565.6 and EBITDA 2,824.6, a 32.0% gross margin and a 20.1% EBITDA margin [S4 p.11, F12, F13, F14, F35]. We set the FY2026E input at 33.7% so that, after the coal and Brent links add 2.0% to cost of revenues, the reported FY2026E gross margin is 32.3% and the year earns the nine-month margin on a fourth quarter whose revenue is seasonally higher (Q4 2025 revenue was 4,814.8 against a 4,305.4 nine-month quarterly average, +11.8%) [S0]. That is the red team's C1 rebase: FY2026E is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the same margin, not a full-year margin that forces a Q4 collapse. FY2027E holds the input and gains from the coal deck falling to 52.5 from 62.0; the input then rises 0.2pp a year to 34.3% by FY2030E as alternative fuels scale to the 42% 2030 target [S4 p.3, p.16]. About 60% of production costs carry some FX exposure [S4 p.12]; the rupiah enters through the cost base, not through a separate driver, so the base carries the house deck path (FY2027E 18,350 against spot 17,968) inside this margin.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: The gross coal share of cost of revenues, entered gross so the pass-through is applied once by the engine. Fuel and power was 4,948.3bn in FY2025, 41.4% of cost of revenues of 11,961.3bn [S2 p.508, F57], and coal is its largest component [S2 p.62]. Alternative fuels reached 33.6% of the fuel mix in 9M2026 from 29.0% [S4 p.16, F24], and the remaining kiln fuel is coal bought domestically; after the alternative-fuel rate and the electricity share of that line, the coal slice of total cost of revenues is 10.8%, which is also the order the listed peer carries. Entered gross, the engine multiplies it by (1 - 75% pass-through), so the net sensitivity is 2.7% of cost of revenues, not the 0.3% the previous 1.2% gross entry implied. The red team's C4 is right that the label said gross while the number was net. This does NOT restore a 20-30% coal beta: the accounts show fuel and power cost per tonne fell 13.4% year on year in 9M2026 while ICI-4 rose [S4 p.12, F25], so a large positive beta is contradicted by the filing; the gross share with the pass-through applied is the defensible middle.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 75%. The 9M2026 profit bridge shows a price effect of -11bn against a volume effect of +221bn [S4 p.13], so cement prices did not carry the fuel move; the company absorbed most of it in the cost base through fuel substitution and contracted supply. With the gross 10.8% share the 25% unpassed residual is a 2.7% net sensitivity of cost of revenues, which the report states; a 20% ICI-4 move therefore shifts EBITDA by roughly two per cent, not the nineteen per cent a no-pass-through gross share would imply — and the accounts do not support the latter.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Brent prices diesel for quarry hauling and road/barge distribution. Delivery, loading and transportation was 2,217bn of selling expense in FY2025, 12.5% of revenue, and sits in operating expense, not cost of revenues [S2 p.173]; the Brent-exposed slice inside COGS itself is the quarry and plant diesel, which we put at 3% of COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 50%, the usual fuel-surcharge pass-through on bulk contracts; the residual 1.5% of COGS carries the Brent deck. Brent is a minor cost line for a coal-fired kiln, so this link moves the margin by well under a percentage point across the forecast.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A operating expense was 21.05% of revenue and 9M2026 21.38% [S0, S4 p.11], of which selling expense (delivery, loading, transport) is the bulk and fell 4.1% in FY2025 on lower volume [S2 p.173]. We hold 21.0% in FY2026E and drift to 20.6% by FY2030E on volume leverage and the distribution efficiency programme, not on a cost cut we cannot see.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK, not the pack: total depreciation, amortisation and depletion was 1,562.9bn in FY2025 and 1,542.9bn in FY2024 [S2 p.482, F3, F4] and 1,267.9bn in 9M2026 [S3 p.62, F23], against a data-pack line of 290.0bn that captured only the operating-expense allocation. On FY2025 revenue that is 8.8%; 9M2026 is 9.0%. We hold the absolute charge near 1,690bn and let the ratio drift down to 8.2% by FY2030E as revenue grows.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set at 8.0% of revenue flat, and the reconciliation the red team asked for, item by item. The company's accrual capex of 1,775bn in FY2025 [F5] splits into 1,252bn of additions to property, plant and equipment and about 523bn of right-of-use additions — of which 296.951bn is land and buildings and 211.366bn machinery and equipment [F43, F44]. The cash-flow statement shows 1,011.7bn paid for fixed assets and intangibles [S2 p.432, S0], so the 251bn balance of the accrual figure is payables timing on the same assets, not a permanent cash saving. The right-of-use additions are non-cash: their cash cost is the lease payment, 494.303bn in FY2025 [F40] and 362.887bn in 9M2026 [F41]. True investment is therefore cash capex plus lease payments: 1,506.0bn, or 8.5% of FY2025 revenue, against the 7.7% the previous draft stated on a 9M lease figure. The 9M2026 run-rate is 529.252bn of cash capex [F42] plus 362.887bn of lease payments [F41], 6.4% of nine-month revenue, so the two anchors bracket 8.0% and we hold it flat: 8.0% is above the five-year average accrual capex of 1,332bn [F5, F6] and below the FY2025 true-investment rate, and it is maintained through the forecast because the DCF formula has no separate lease line and the lease liability is already in net debt. The alternative accrual treatment (right-of-use additions in capex, no lease payments) gives the FY2025 10.0% [F5] and a lower FCFF. The substantive point the red team raised is that the FCFF line had no lease treatment at all, and this is it: the lease payment is inside capex, stated here so the reader can re-cut it.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net working capital was 3.7% of revenue at the FY2025A close and 5.2% on the pack's three-year average; the company itself reports working capital over revenue of 5.7% at 9M2026 [S4 p.14], so the 9M actual is above our 5.2%, not below it. The red team's 3.7% is the year-end point: a cement business' receivables and payables swing around the year-end. Holding 5.2%, between the year-end and the nine-month actual, is not a conservative bias — it is above the last full-year close.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A effective tax was 17.8% of reported PBT and the 9M2026 rate is 19.9% [S0, S4 p.11]; the statutory rate is 22% and the company benefits from incentives. Set 19.5%, between the two observed rates and just below the nine-month actual, so this is not a conservative haircut.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of 111.9bn in 9M2026 on average bank debt of about 1.5-2.0trn and lease liabilities imply roughly 6-7% [S3 p.9, p.5]. Set 6.5%, the pack's three-year average, appropriate for a net-cash investment-grade-style borrower.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The pack's three-year average of interest income over opening cash, 4.25% [S0], is consistent with Indonesian time-deposit rates with the BI rate at 5.75% [deck].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing assumed: net cash of about 1.2trn at the June 2026 balance sheet and 2.2trn at September [S0, S3 F21, F22, F30], and the company funds capex and dividends from operating cash flow.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: 45bn a year: the share of net profit of associates was 37bn in FY2025 and 49.8bn in 9M2026 [S2 p.168, S4 p.11], offset by the small other expense line. The FY2025 one-off gain of 670bn on the divestment and remeasurement of an associate is excluded from every forecast year [S2 p.168].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: profit attributable to non-controlling interests was nil in FY2025 and FY2024 [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The reported payout history is 43.2% for FY2024 and 15.8% for FY2023 when capex was higher, and 68% for FY2025 on reported profit (1,536.227bn paid in June 2026 [F26] on 2,248.781bn). Excluding the 670bn associate one-off [F38], the FY2025 DPS of 468 was about 97% of clean EPS. The red team's C6 is right that 75% cut the cash dividend against that record without a source, and that because the roll subtracts next-twelve-month DPS a low payout mechanically lifts the price target. We hold 90%, between the clean 97% and the reported 68%: on FY2026E EPS it pays a DPS above the 468 actually paid, the balance sheet is net cash of about 2.2trn at September [F21, F22, F30] and cash capex runs below depreciation, so a near-full distribution is what the record supports; 90% rather than 97% leaves the retention the P-14 and Grobogan programmes need. §4 states that the DPS is subtracted in the roll and added back in the total return, so the payout is a split between price and income, not a value.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -0.65%: issued and paid-up shares fell to 3,283,558,399 at 30 September 2026 from 3,305,110,399 at 31 December 2025, a further 21,552,000 treasury shares cancelled in 2026 on top of the 165,628,900 cancelled in 2025 [S3 p.104, S2 p.12, F45]. That reconciles the FY2025 cash dividend of 1,536.227bn to the 468 DPS on 3,283.6m shares [F26, S0], which is the count the DCF and the market capitalisation use. Nil after FY2026E: no further cancellation is announced.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, set equal to the explicit nominal revenue growth the forecast already carries in FY2031E-FY2035E (volume in the low single digits plus a price path roughly flat in real terms), so the terminal value no longer grows faster than the years before it: the red team is right that 3.5% did. It is also below the macro deck's Indonesian CPI of 3.28% [deck] and well inside the house cap. Cement demand grows with GDP but the industry has been overbuilt for a decade and price has not kept pace with inflation [S4 p.5, S7], so a terminal rate at or below the explicit path is the most likely long-run outcome, not a haircut.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E was never rebased to the 9M actuals, so the annual model earns a 19.43% EBITDA margin against the 20.07% the company just printed; that forces a Q4 EBITDA margin of 17.7% on Q4 revenue of 5,307.3bn (19,378.1 less 14,070.8) versus 20.07% for the nine months. Section 3 presents this as the fourth quarter being at the nine-month quarterly average, which is true only at the EBITDA line because Q4 revenue is assumed 13% above the nine-month quarterly average. Nothing in S4 or S7 sources a Q4 margin fall while fuel and power cost per tonne fell 13.4%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2026E is rebuilt as the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month 20.1% EBITDA margin on its seasonally higher revenue: FY2026E EBITDA is now 3,894.3 at 20.1% rather than 3,764.4 at 19.4%, so no Q4 margin compression remains. The gross-margin input was re-anchored so the reported margin after the cost links equals the nine-month print [S4 p.11, F14, F35].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states a multiple should be struck on the through-cycle path, quotes through-cycle EBITDA of 4,461.1bn, and then strikes the EV/EBITDA leg on the trough LTM figure of 3,599.8bn. At the same 4.89x peer median on 4,461.1 the leg is about 7,550 a share rather than 6,275, worth roughly 360 rupiah on the target at the 0.25 weight after the roll.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on the value, accepted on the text. The engine strikes both multiple legs on trailing last-twelve-month earnings, which is what the peer medians are measured on; the paragraph claimed a through-cycle strike and contradicted itself, and that sentence is deleted. We do not move the leg to through-cycle EBITDA because applying a mid-cycle multiple to through-cycle EBITDA while the peer set is measured on trailing earnings mixes two cycles inside one cross-check. The DCF carries the cycle at 60% of the weight, and §4 states the convention once [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative names rupiah depreciation, coal staying high and selling costs that do not flex, but the shock list is volume 0.95, price 0.94, gross margin -2.5pp and capex 1.25 only: there is no FX driver in the template and the coal link is 0.3% of COGS, so two of the named mechanisms do nothing. The -2.5pp gross-margin shock is not anchored to any stated historical trough even though the report calls the price war high-likelihood and high-impact, and the distribution-cost regulation described in section 2 has no quantified shock.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Both wings now shock the same four drivers, mirrored: volume 0.95/1.05, price 0.94/1.06, gross margin -2/+2pp and opex +2/-2pp; the capex shock is dropped. The bear's FX and coal mechanisms are now stated to run through the gross-margin shock because the template has no rupiah series and a standalone ICI-4 shock is worth only a couple of per cent of EBITDA. The gross-margin shock takes the reported margin below the FY2022 five-year trough in the annual report, deliberately [S2 p.13, S7].

challenges.challenge: link1_share of 0.012 is the gross COGS share in the engine formula revenue x (1 - gm) x (1 + share x (1 - pass) x (ICI-4 change)), so the net coal linkage is 1.2% x 25% = 0.3% of COGS. The analyst own basis says fuel and power is 43% of COGS and the gross coal slice is roughly a quarter of that, about 10.8%, and the cement peer BLES carries 12%. A 20% ICI-4 move therefore changes INTP EBITDA by about 79bn (2%) where the stated basis implies about 715bn (19%), and the summary claim that the coal deck is one of the things that moves the value is not true of the model as built.
challenges.answer: Accepted. link1_share is now the gross coal share of cost of revenues, 10.8% -- fuel and power 4,948.3bn, 41.4% of FY2025 cost of revenues [S2 p.508, F57], after the 33.6% alternative-fuel rate [S4 p.16, F24] -- with the 75% pass-through applied once, a 2.7% net exposure. The gross-margin input is re-anchored so FY2026E still prints the nine-month 32.3% reported margin. A 20% ICI-4 move is now worth a low-single-digit percentage of EBITDA, not 19%, because the filing shows fuel and power cost per tonne down 13.4% year on year while ICI-4 rose [S4 p.12, F25]; the thesis and risk ranking say so.

challenges.challenge: The P/BV leg at 0.327x is set on a peer median the assumptions themselves describe as a mix of cement with construction and property names (WTON, WSBP, BEBS, AYLS, SOLA, BATR). On the model own ROE of 8%, COE of 12.4% and g of 2.5% the justified P/B is about 0.56x, and at 0.56x the leg would be about 3,880 a share rather than 2,273, worth roughly 270 rupiah on the target. The assumptions also set multiple_source peer_median while operating configuration sets CEMENT to blend, yet section 4 calls the weights and policy the industry defaults.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part. The peer-median P/BV leg is kept, but the override of the CEMENT default blend is now documented with its value effect instead of being called industry policy, and §4 puts the justified P/B, (ROE - g)/(COE - g) on ROE 7.5%, COE 12.4% and g 2.5%, beside the 0.33x peer median. We do not switch to blend because the own-history EV/EBITDA mean is more than twice the peer median and would put that leg above the DCF, the mid-cycle-multiple-on-trough error [S0].

challenges.challenge: The base case payout of 75% gives DPS of 399 against the 468 actually paid, a 15% dividend cut with no source, while the assumptions compute the FY2025 payout at about 97% of clean EPS (1,536.227bn paid per F26 on 2,248.781bn profit less the 670bn associate gain per F38). Because the target subtracts next-12m DPS from the rolled value, the low payout mechanically raises the value: at 97% net cash would be about 387bn lower, the DCF about 118 a share lower and the target about 200 rupiah lower, so the apparently cautious choice is worth about 3% of the target and 1.4pp of the 29.0% total return.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Payout is raised to 90%, which pays DPS of 510.8 against the 468 actually paid on FY2025, so there is no dividend cut; §4 now states that next-twelve-month DPS is subtracted in the roll and added back in the total return, so the payout is a price-versus-income choice. The target falls by about 130 as a result of the change [F26, S3 p.9].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 asserts the company is not on the exchange special monitoring board and carries no special notation, cited to S0, a Yahoo Finance statements and price feed. That source cannot evidence an IDX board status or notation letter, and the earnings-quality card makes board status a gate before any thesis.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The S0 citation is withdrawn and replaced with the annual report's own statement that there was no temporary suspension of trading nor delisting during 2025 and no material capital-market administrative sanction, recorded as fact F60 [S2 p.17, p.373]. idx.co.id is outside the fetch registry, so the exchange notation list itself cannot be archived; §3 says the board status rests on the company's disclosure rather than pretending a price feed evidences it.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the September balance sheet carries more net cash than the year-end roll so the multiple on the valuation-date figures is lower. The model shows the opposite: September net non-operating assets are 2,991.2bn (2,738.6 cash less loans plus 837.1 associates less 584.4 leases) against FY2026E year-end net cash of 3,138.9bn, so the September multiple is the higher one (4.09x versus 4.05x).
challenges.answer: Accepted. The direction was reversed: September net cash of 2,154.1bn is lower than the FY2026E roll's 3,243.5bn, so the multiple on the valuation-date figures is higher, not lower. §4 now says so and calls the target effect a rounding error [S3, F21, F22, F30].

challenges.challenge: Two share counts are in use: the model shares line and the EPS/DPS path use 3,305.1m while the DCF and the market cap use 3,283.6m. The FY2025 payment settles it: 1,536.227bn divided by the 468 DPS is 3,283.6m, so the EPS and DPS in the model are about 0.65% low and the per-share paths do not agree.
challenges.answer: Accepted. share_change for FY2026E is set to -0.6515% to the September count of 3,283,558,399 shares [S3 p.79], which is the count the dividend payment implies; EPS, DPS, DCF and market capitalisation now all use 3,283.6m and FY2026E DPS is 510.8 on EPS 567.5.

challenges.challenge: The 210.5m treasury shares (5.99% of shares, carried at 105.2bn of cost per the S2 note and F45) are dismissed as option value in the bull case without a number, although cancelling them would lift EPS about 6% for a consideration that is 0.6% of market cap and the company has already cancelled 165.6m shares.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The treasury block is quantified in the bull: 210.5m shares, 5.99% of the count, carried at 105.2bn of cost, lifting EPS by roughly that share on cancellation at under one per cent of market capitalisation [F58, F59, S2 p.109]. It stays outside base and bull because no further cancellation is announced beyond the September count, and the base already uses that count [S3 p.79].

challenges.challenge: Section 2 describes the West Java two-axle limit and zero-ODOL enforcement as distribution cost and logistics risks but the model carries no distribution-cost line beyond a flat 21.0% opex ratio drifting down to 20.6%, and no scenario shocks opex. A one-point rise in opex to revenue is about 194bn of EBITDA, 5% of FY2026E.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Bear and bull now carry an opex shock of plus or minus two points of revenue, mirrored; a one-point rise is about 194bn of EBITDA, around five per cent of FY2026E, so this is the channel that carries the West Java two-axle limit and zero-ODOL enforcement [S2 p.57, S7]. The risk section states the exposure and the shock.

challenges.challenge: The report prints a 29.3% domestic market share and, from the same Q3 deck, a 48.1 Mt nine-month national market against 15.087 Mt of domestic volume, which is 31.4%. The forecast volume of 21.7 Mt is 32.5% of the deck 2026E demand of 66.8 Mt, not 29.3%, so the claim that the company holds its share rests on a share metric that is 2-3pp below the volume arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Accepted. §2 now states the denominator: the company's reported 29.3% is its own market definition, while domestic volume of 15.087 Mt against the deck's 48.132 Mt nine-month market is a share in the low thirties [S4 p.8, p.11]. The forecast volume of 21.7 Mt is about a third of the deck's 66 Mt FY2026E demand, so the base assumes the share the nine-month volume already earns, not a stable 29.3%, and the text no longer calls the forecast share-neutral.

missing_bull_case.note: The EV/EBITDA leg is struck at 4.89x on trough LTM EBITDA of 3,599.8 immediately after section 4 says a multiple should be struck on the through-cycle 4,461.1 (leg would be ~7,550 not 6,275). The 210.5m treasury shares (5.99%) are called option value and never quantified although cancellation is worth ~6% of EPS at a 105bn cost. Base volume adopts the deck 3%/yr for FY2027+ after 9M2026 ran 7.9%.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear shocks (volume 0.95, price 0.94, GM -2.5pp, capex 1.25) contain neither the rupiah depreciation nor the coal-stays-high mechanism its own narrative names, and the model has no FX driver and only a 0.3%-of-COGS coal link, so the text is deeper than the model. No historical trough margin is cited for the -2.5pp, and the two-axle and zero-ODOL distribution cost described in section 2 carries no quantified downside.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E annual inputs were not rebased to the 9M actuals: the model full-year EBITDA margin of 19.43% against the 9M actual of 20.07% forces a Q4 EBITDA margin of 17.7% on Q4 revenue of 5,307.3bn, a 2.4pp fall with no source while fuel and power cost per tonne printed -13.4%. Gross margin 31.7% vs 32.0% actual; opex 21.0% vs 21.4% actual is the one optimistic line.

Section 2 prints a 29.3% domestic share and, from the same deck, a 48.1 Mt nine-month market that implies 31.4%. Verified verbatim instead: F3 D&A note at S2 p.482, F30 leases 443.441 plus 140.988 equals 584.429, F22/F48 short-term loans 2,000 with no long-term bank loan, S7 122/66/45-46%, associates 837.098 at S3 p.4, and 165.6m shares cancelled at S2 p.7.

Arithmetic that does tie: net cash 2,738.6 plus associates 837.1 less leases 584.4 equals 2,991.2, matching the pack debt of 2,584.4 once leases are split, and the -369 EV / -111 DCF / -67 blend / -70 target roll reproduces exactly.
